record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some numerical results are described only through figures; no plotted values are transcribed.
record.tranche_reason: The paper develops and evaluates a theoretical account that refines scaling laws: the exponent depends on spectral redundancy and target smoothness, and finite-width approximation can produce departures from a power law. It does not reproduce large-language-model scaling sweeps or test compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical excess-risk results and synthetic/kernel experiments, including representation changes, dependence, mixtures, and finite-width random features. It does not report held-out cross-entropy measurements on pretrained language models, parameter/token/compute scaling sweeps, downstream-task results, or a compute-optimal parameter/token split. General background claims and cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: A theoretical paper with synthetic kernel-regression experiments. It derives excess-risk power laws in sample size from an assumed polynomial spectral tail. It never measures any neural model's loss against parameters, tokens or compute, in language or any other modality. The Transformer results (Theorems 6–7) assume a power-law NTK tail, so they presuppose rather than test the form. Kernel ridge regression and random Fourier features on synthetic Gaussian data are a different kind of system from the ones V1–V7 name. The paper's argument that exponents depend on data (β, s) bears on V7 only by analogy. The findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors claim to prove that scaling laws are redundancy laws: the exponent α=2s/(2s+1/β) is set by the spectral tail and target smoothness. They claim universality across bounded transforms, mixtures, finite width and Transformer (NTK and drift) regimes, presented as explaining empirical scaling across NLP and CV. In Limitations they concede that the work is purely theoretical, without validation on real datasets, and that the Transformer results rest on strong assumptions.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses kernel-regression theory, synthetic experiments, and assumption-based Transformer analyses rather than empirical language-model parameter/token/compute sweeps or held-out cross-entropy measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The exponent depends on the spectral-tail index β and target smoothness s. Dependence changes curve position against raw n but the reported curves collapse when plotted against neff. Finite-width deviations vary with feature width m; the paper reports closer alignment for m ≥ 1000 and approximation-noise dominance for m = 50 and 100.

fits_no_version.finding: In kernel ridge regression under a polynomial spectral tail (β) and source condition (s), the optimal excess risk is proven to scale as n^-α with α=2s/(2s+1/β). Synthetic Gaussian experiments (Fig 7a–c) show the fitted slope close to 0.67 at β=2, s=0.5, and steeper curves with larger s or β.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In kernel regression, the data-scaling exponent is set by the spectral-tail index and target smoothness, so exponents are not universal.

fits_no_version.finding: In synthetic kernel experiments, bounded invertible representation transforms leave the slope unchanged. AR(1) dependence shifts curves, which then collapse against neff. A two-component spectral mixture follows the heavier tail (min β).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Kernel-regression learning-curve exponents are invariant to bounded reparametrisation and to short-range dependence, and are dominated by the heaviest spectral tail in mixtures.

fits_no_version.finding: Random Fourier feature models with widths m=50–2000 follow the power law at small n but show intermediate-n humps. Widths m≥1000 align more closely with the kernel law. Theory gives a sufficient width condition m ≳ n^{r/(2s+1/β)}.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Finite-width random-feature approximations bend learning curves away from a single power law unless width grows polynomially with n.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorems 6–7 assert that Transformer excess risk follows n^-α if the NTK (or the time-averaged kernel) has a polynomial tail. This is derived from assumptions, with no experiment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Conditional theoretical account of Transformer data scaling via the NTK spectral tail.

record.problems: The paper states that it is purely theoretical and lacks numerical validation on real datasets. The Transformer results rely on assumptions about polynomial NTK tails, ridge-equivalent early stopping, tail stability, and adiabatic kernel drift. Several experimental curves are figure-only, without numerical slopes, risks, or uncertainty estimates.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T5' with V5/V7 support labels is not justified. Every experiment uses synthetic kernel or random-feature regression, and the Transformer theorems assume the power-law spectrum they conclude from. No row measures a neural model's loss against model size, data or compute in any modality. The paper also only scales sample size n, never parameters or compute in the V1/V3 sense. Several 'partial' states in the record (e.g. r8) mismatched the reported results.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy measurements on language models; no separate sweeps over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No fits from small runs are used to predict the loss of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between model parameters and training tokens is evaluated.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count. Representation transforms are not architecture-shape comparisons.

The paper studies theoretical kernel/Transformer settings and synthetic experiments, not empirical scaling in image or video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer; it does not establish the claim for real-world modalities or training regimes.
No downstream-task performance is measured or predicted.

The paper shows dependence on spectral-tail index and target smoothness, and reports finite-width curve deviations. It does not test parameter-counting choices, alternative fitting procedures, training schedules, or compute-optimal allocation fits.
